utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-02-65-PT, the Prosecutor versus Zeljko Mejakic, Momcilo Gruban, Dusan Fustar, Dusko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I have the appearances. The Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Susan L. Somers, senior trial attorney for the Office of the Prosecutor, along with Ms. Ann Sutherland, trial attorney, and Mr. Sebastian van Hooydonk, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Then for the Defence. May I first have the appearances for Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. Jovan Simic, an attorney from Belgrade, and my colleague Zoran Zivanovic, appearing for Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Branko Lukic and I am representing Mr. Momcilo Gruban, who is not with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Then the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Theodore Scudder, here with Dragan Ivetic. We represent the defendant Dusan Fustar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scudder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. Slobodanka Nedic, attorney at law, appearing for Dusko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nedic. Then we have invited the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of Serbia. Who will present themselves first? Will it be Serbia and Montenegro or will it -- I think it's proper since Bosnia and Herzegovina is -- there is a motion for referral. I'll say a bit more about that at a later stage. There is a motion for referral of these cases to Bosnia and Herzegovina, so therefore Bosnia and Herzegovina is directly, by force of this motion, involved in this case. So may I have the appearances for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. My name is Meddzida Kreso, I am the president of the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And with me is Ms. Fidelma Donlon, the deputy registrar of the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. My name is Vaso Marinkovic. I am the deputy chief state prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina dealing with war crimes, and to my right is my colleague Mr. Nicholas Koumjian, also an international prosecutor for war crimes in the state prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marinkovic. Thank you, Ms. Kreso. Then for Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. My name is Zoran Loncar. I am a minister in the government of the Republic of Serbia and a member of the National Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. With me today to my left is Mr. Branislav Ristivojevic, an advisor, and to my right, Mr. Bogdan Stankovic, the deputy prosecutor for war crimes of the Republic of Serbia. Next to him is Mr. Sasa Obradovic, the first secretary of the embassy of Serbia and Montenegro here in The Hague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loncar. I hope that I'll not mix up your names during this hearing. I hope you'll have some understanding for it. But let me first ask the accused who are present whether they can hear me in a language you understand. I add to that that the only thing that was said until now was that everyone presented themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MEJAKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your name is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MEJAKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zeljko Mejakic, and I am the first accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mejakic. And next to you sits?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dusko Knezevic and I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FUSTAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dusan Fustar, and I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Fustar. So we now know at least who is in this courtroom. In this courtroom we'll hear today the further submissions from the parties in relation to a motion - a motion filed by the Prosecution - for referral of the cases against the four accused, Mr. Gruban not being present today but represented, a referral of the cases in order to be -- to have them further prosecuted then tried in the Republic of -- Bosnia and Herzegovina. I already alluded for a very short moment to the presence of the representatives of the -- of Serbia and Montenegro. That is because Defence counsel have drawn the attention of your government to the fact that this motion was pending before this court and you have requested the court whether you could make any submissions here, and out of courtesy, although as I said before, you are not a party to these proceedings, the Chamber is interested to hear the submissions you would like to make. We'll hear today, therefore, the further submissions of the parties. The Chamber has read carefully all the submissions made in writing until now. We have asked very specific questions, both to Defence, Prosecution, and to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, if -- I'll allow you in a second to make further submissions. I would not mind if the parties would very briefly summarise, because this is a public hearing, very briefly summarise their positions. But the Chamber is more interested to hear, apart from any important addition to the submissions you made already, but the Chamber is very much interested to hear what your reply, response, reaction is to what the other interested parties in this case have submitted to the Court so that we are better able to understand where exactly the problems are. Therefore, I would first like to give an opportunity to the Prosecution to make further submissions in respect of its motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I first, as a threshold inquiry, ask if any aspect of confidentiality that was affixed to the Prosecution's initial submissions has been lifted because this is -- I'm sorry, the Defence, has been lifted for this hearing so that we can respond in open court to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any -- there -- when we discuss matters of confidentiality, I would like to invite you to keep that for a moment, because if there is any confidentiality involved, then whether or not to lift that, if it would need any discussion, then of course we have to do that in the presence of the direct parties to the case only. If any confidentiality that is claimed by the Defence or is asked for by the Defence would be lifted, then of course we would hear from the Defence now and then you could feel free. But otherwise, I would like to ask you to keep it for a moment that we can go in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would also ask at this moment, just to bring to the Chamber's attention, a point of corrigenda which I think will be helpful before I commence the very brief summary of the status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the Prosecution's submissions of 21 February, 2005, in footnotes 12, 19, 25, and 39, there was a citation to a provision of the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Unfortunately, we did not at the time have the number. We can now inform the Chamber that it is 61/04.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, by way of brief summary as to how we are here today: On 2nd September, 2004, the Prosecution filed its request under Rule 11 bis for referral to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in response the counsel for the various defendants -- and of course the case was a four-accused case. Responses have come in. There was a request by this Chamber for further comment, I believe on the 9th of February. And on the 21st of February, if I'm correct as to the date, the Prosecution submitted additional comments pursuant to the Chamber's order of 9 February. The -- again, by very brief summary for purposes of the record, this case emanates from the events of the -- what are referred to as the Omarska and Keraterm camp atrocities in 1992 in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The issues that must be presented to this Court are on the gravity of the offence and on the level of the accused. The Prosecution stands on its submissions that the gravity of the offence, and of course it acknowledges that in order to be in this Tribunal or before this Tribunal the offences are grave, they are of the utmost seriousness. Acknowledging the mandate of the Security Council that, even bearing that in mind, some of these serious cases must be referred to other Tribunals. The level of the accused, reiterating that in the context of this extremely serious criminal enterprise, as it has been referred to, Omarska, and of course the similar criminality at Keraterm, in this context the level of the accused, albeit high within that context, is such that in the overall scheme of let's say a criminal continuum, we believe it would be deemed as to some lower, and as to, for example, accused Mejakic, mid-level. Again, entirely appropriate for referral under Rule 11 bis. The other considerations as to fairness, and the up-and-running structures available in Bosnia and Herzegovina have been set forth. As a point of introduction, I don't know how much detail Your Honour would like me to go into, but if this suffices for purposes of background procedural history, then I would stop here and then pick up where additional questioning will be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be sufficient. Then I'd like to -- well, when I say it's sufficient, I of course also invited you to touch upon those subjects that have specifically been raised in the written submissions, so even before we would have perhaps specific questions for you, if there would be any issue raised by any of the parties that you would like to address, you may do so now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, of course in general the opposition by all accused to the motion has been the springing point from which we have looked at response. I'd like to point out that one of the concerns that had been raised, which is about the concept of anonymous witness, the use of the term, has been cured. It now -- the reference, and I believe the esteemed members of the delegation from Bosnia and Herzegovina can further go into it, the reference now is to nondisclosure of certain things, more in line with the concept that I think has been used -- well, I know has been used before this Tribunal. So that whole notion of anonymity is not a concern at this point in time. The issue of keeping accused together for trial is of course one that we think is extremely important and hence we believe it entirely appropriate that all four accused should be referred to the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina for this proceeding. Issues of other possible venues raised by virtue of having the Government of Serbia and Montenegro make an appearance, albeit that was certainly not contemplated by the Prosecution, I think are irrelevant. The issue is: These persons allegedly committed the crimes on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; it is the most appropriate forum. It has a court set up now, a very specialised court, which is able and willing and eager to handle this case, eager in the sense of its preparedness. And we see that there should be no need to look further for a jurisdiction, particularly in this -- under these facts and given that all were born in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that any relationship to Serbia and Montenegro I would have to describe as tangential in that they have been given, at various points in time, indicia of citizenship, and it is our position that it was for convenience as opposed to anything else. That in fact how they came to this Tribunal can be characterised not as an avenue of reward; they have an obligation to come to this Tribunal. And they were not arrested in the true sense of the word, but in fact that any consideration should be given for the nature of how they came here I think is also irrelevant. That they may have come from the territory of Serbia and Montenegro should not be of a concern for this Tribunal. What is of a concern is that a good portion of the witness base will be from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The nature of the case should also be considered. And that the stage at which the preparations find themselves would make it ideally suited for this referral. Excuse me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Issues were raised, Your Honours, about witnesses for the Defence and if there are any -- if this may be more appropriately the subject of private or closed -- private session, I am certainly willing to defer any discussion on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you better not at this moment until we have discussed with the parties what they would like to raise in private session. Is there any other matter you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The concerns that were raised about current Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- that will certainly be handled by the appropriate officials in Bosnia and Herzegovina who are mindful of the need to expeditiously make sure these cases go to trial. And there is -- as our understanding from what we have read, the realm of discretion necessary to ensure that. We believe that part of their willingness and ability to accept this case is the understood good faith in making sure that things move forward quickly -- or expeditiously, I should say, and however the appointment of counsel aspect of moving things forward expeditiously factors into a plan I am confident will be addressed in great detail with great concern by the Registry. It appears that the element of discretion works in favour of these counsel, if it is deemed appropriate, being able to continue representation. Again, I think our learned friends from Bosnia-Herzegovina can best address that. But from our perspective, that does not present a problem. I think I have been succinct on these points. And if there comes a point where an issue is raised by my learned friends later, I would ask for the Court's indulgence in letting me address them as they arise. There were so many sub-issues that I think I would be more effective if I have the Chamber's permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers, for this first -- the first matters you have addressed. I would like to give an opportunity to the Defence to make further submissions. Until now we have -- this Chamber has received submissions on the one hand for Mr. Mejakic and then submissions by the three other counsel for the other accused. Is this what we can expect this afternoon as well? Are the -- Mr. Simic, I take it that you'll make submissions on behalf of Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of all the accused have agreed to divide the topics among us in order to save time. The introductory remarks will be made by Mr. Scudder, I will follow him, and hen we will deal with each topic one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, of course, highly appreciates that you have found an efficient way of dealing with problems that are similar for your clients. Mr. Scudder, may I give you an opportunity to make the introductory submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am Theodore Scudder, with Mr. Ivetic, representing Mr. Fustar. As Mr. Simic has said, we have tried to save time and repetition here by each addressing certain of the issues that have been raised. I would like to speak particularly about this case, which does not seem to be appropriate for a transfer or to lend itself readily to this type of a transfer. Ms. Somers mentioned keeping the four defendants together, but there have been other defendants tried on basically the same facts already here at the ICTY, which I think affects what is being done here. I would like to first make one correction. There is a reference to the defendants have been born in Bosnia. The defendant Dusan Fustar was born in Serbia and had gone back to Serbia just before he surrendered himself. He had made attempts, through both governments, to surrender himself and ended up surrendering himself directly to the UN. My comments about this case are in contrast to the usual case. I think the people that have written the rules probably had in mind a case where the defendants would be together in preparation for a case and in standing trial, and this case is quite different. We're dealing with several different times and places. First of all, there are the two different camps, Keraterm and Omarska. As the Court knows, there was an initial trial of three people labelled Keraterm 1. It resulted, after trial, in convictions of the defendants Sikirica, Dosen and Kolundzija. In fact, some of their sentences had been completely served before other people in the same case surrendered themselves and Keraterm 2 started. And in the meantime there was also an Omarska case with five defendants, Kvocka, Prcac, Kos, Zigic and Radic. And now the facts of that case are involved in the present matter also. There have been related cases also; the first one against Dusko Tadic. There is a case on which the appeal is still pending on Milomar Stakic, and of course we have the four defendants in this case who were once five. There was also Predrag Banovic, who pled guilty and was included in the same indictment. So there have been at least 12 people involved in the overall fact situation. The Prosecution and the amended indictment have described a joint criminal enterprise including all of the people that I have just named. And so in terms of keeping people together, we already have an established situation where this court has dealt with all of them up to this time. Considering the three years or more of preparation just on the people before this Court now, there is a great investment of time and effort that has already been put in by the Prosecution and their investigators, by the Defence, and also by the Court. And consequently, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there is a large amount of accumulated evidence relating to the facts, particularly the matters mentioned by Ms. Somers, namely the seriousness of the offence and the overall joint criminal enterprise charged and also facts that would indicate the relative culpability, not only of the four people before the Court now but also of those others that I mentioned. Any new personnel from another jurisdiction coming into this case will have a considerable body of evidence and background information to digest and build on. And really, at this point it would be practically impossible I think - and I speak from my own experience as a lawyer for 40 years, including ten years as a prosecutor in the United States and years as a criminal defence attorney - it's very difficult for lawyers, prosecution or defence, to pick up a case that's been developed by other people and know it as well or feel as comfortable with it. So any new court, including all of the personnel, would be at some considerable disadvantage, not to mention disadvantages to the defendants themselves who have been dealing with a particular court and body of evidence being developed. Three of the four defendants before this court surrendered themselves before Rule 11 was ever amended the first of three times to come into its current form. It has also been mentioned, as we've learned via Florence Hartmann on behalf of the OTP, that the Prosecution feels there should be consideration where people voluntarily surrender themselves, and particularly when they do so promptly and early, as has been done in this case. This has several resulting consequences for us, I believe. First of all, there's a problem of consistency. If this case were to be transferred elsewhere, we would end up with people involved in the crimes charged here where there would be the judgements I've already mentioned here at the ICTY and then a different judgement by a different court with different personnel operating under different rules in a different place. That would leave open the possibility that people would seek inconsistencies between the two judgements, they would point out any inconsistencies in sentencing, it could forum shopping, and make it difficult to operate with the transfer rules in the future in other cases of a more usual type. There is also the matter of judicial economy. I mentioned how much time has been spent developing this case. I believe we were told a year ago that it was ready for trial here, and anybody starting up in a new jurisdiction would be repeating a lot of work that has already been done. I will take as an example one thing that I believe illustrates my comments, and that is that the current Stakic case on appeal has raised some issue about the maximum sentence that can be imposed in this court. If this case before this court were transferred and another court started applying its own rules, there's the possibility that a ruling could be made on that issue in the Stakic case and a question raised whether the transferee court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: -- here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Scudder, could you please slow down because the interpretation has some difficulties -- not in following you but in translating you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: Right. I'm trying to wrap it up here. My point is that with decisions made in one group of facts and two different courts, there would be problems raised, both as to judicial economy and, more importantly, to consistency which relates to the two matters mentioned in Rule 11, both the severity of sentence, whether the new court -- the severity of the crime, whether the new court would see the severity the same way, and also particularly the relative culpability among the individual defendants. The ICTY has already considered other people involved at both Keraterm and Omarska during the same events that are involved in this case, and so the Prosecution and Defence both have some good sense of the relative culpability among the people. And I might mention, I believe at least two of the people before the court now have been involved in some effort to settle their case, and that of course is based on knowledge of both the Prosecution and the Defence of the relative culpability of the crimes they are charged with and the evidence to support it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm re-reading your last line about some effort. If there's any information that we need to know in order to make no mistakes, any further information, we'll hear from you. Mr. Scudder, thank you. You, Mr. Simic, will be the next one who will address the Court on the next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It is the view of all the Defence counsel in order for Rule 11 bis to apply, the Trial Chamber needs to determine whether all conditions will be met for a fair trial. Furthermore, the Defence would like to discuss certain standards that it deems need to be met. I will just mention them briefly. We should not be guided by financial or political reasons to determine whether this case should be referred or not, but we should be guided by the principles of justice, a fair trial, and all the other provisions in Rule 11 bis, and the Trial Chamber should base its decision in this matter on criminal substantive and procedural law in the country where the trial would be conducted. The first basic precondition is a fair trial. The provisions in Article 14 of the International Covenant on Human Rights and Article 6 of the European Convention of Human Rights are the basic provisions that we have to meet. We will not be listing all of them. We will just focus on those elements that indicate that it would be highly problematic that the conduct of a fair trial would be a highly problematic thing. First of all, it is a provision that the Court must be unbiased and independent. It is difficult to say to what extent a court is independent or dependent and it is difficult to say whether a court is indeed free of all pressure. It has been proven -- international case law indicates, for instance, in the US courts many of the cases you have changes of venue or, for instance, in the Lockerbie case, the venue had been changed to Holland in order to ensure a fair trial. This is something that the Security Council Resolution 955 determined, where it is indicated that the -- in a certain -- in a certain case the trial had to be held in another country because the trial could not be independent. This is a general situation. We are not talking about the persons working there, but we also have to take into account the general security situation in the country where the trial is to be held. Bosnia and Herzegovina continues to be a high-risk site. The Security Council recommendation is not to -- the state department recommends to its citizens not to travel to Bosnia and Herzegovina without undue need. Conditions indeed have not been met there, despite the fact that the war is over, for the troops that are there to withdraw, and we also have the situation where Mr. Paddy Ashdown, the high representative, has the highest authority and he has the final say in all aspects of public life and political life. He can even ban certain people from having public functions and political functions. Organised crime is rife. Let me give you an example. Dragan Coric, the Supreme Court -- president of the Supreme Court, and another judge have been accused of having been involved in organised crime. There are some other cases in which persons have been indicted for abuse of office. In Bosnia and Herzegovina organised terrorist groups have been proven to exist there, and various other organisations are also active there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you think that it of -- it would be of great assistance to the Chamber to hear all the shortcomings of whatever state that was involved -- that might be involved in a referral, either in this case or in future cases? We have requests pending, for example, to refer a case to Serbia and Montenegro. Do you think that it would assist us in that case to hear whatever is wrong in the governments, society, economics of that state? Would that all be so important to take into consideration to consider whether a trial could be fair? I mean, you said that the -- I'm not aware of it, but that in the United States they say, Don't travel to Bosnia and Herzegovina; it's not a safe place. Do you expect us to compare whether there are similar recommendations made by other governments to their citizens? Is that not a bit far away from what it is really about and which you started, and that is whether there could be a fair trial? I could mention you a lot of states where sooner or later government officials would be involved in bribery, corruption. Not necessarily all these states disqualify as states that could have a good legal system. I'm not saying they have, but I just wonder to what extent it is relevant what you're drawing our attention to at this moment. Would you please keep this in mind if you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The idea of the Defence was to note certain aspects that might be relevant and that, in my opinion, should be presented to the Trial Chamber when making the decision whether the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina could operate without any pressure. I will wrap up. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ethnic, political, and religious intolerance is rife. This has been noted by Europe Union institutions. There is a media campaign preparing for a trial of the Omarska case, and after all, we must keep in mind that the Omarska camp case is the one that has been the most present in the media of all the cases. After all, Omarska and the Vukovar crimes led to the establishment of this Tribunal quite sooner than expected. As we noted in our briefs, all parties in these proceedings stated that it is quite difficult to find anyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina who has not had -- who has not been affected by the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. What we wanted to say is that the demands of the fair trial do not coincide always with the demands to try a case where the crime was committed. We've already noted the Rwanda situation and all the other cases, and it is our concern that this animosity against the accused in the place where the crimes were committed might affect the fairness of the trial, it might affect the accused, the Defence counsel, and perhaps the Court itself, the Judges themselves. Likewise, the accused have the right to be tried without undue delay. Judge Robinson noted that the Trial Chamber is ready to proceed with trial, and the Prosecution and the Defence agreed with that. The Prosecution estimated that it would need four to six weeks for its case and the Defence would probably not need much longer. The question then is whether it is indeed fair to extend the detention of these accused who have been in detention for two or maybe even four years awaiting trial. The provisions of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina stipulate what is considered to be a trial without undue delay. The Criminal Procedure Code stipulates that the indictment needs to be adapted to the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means that we have further deadlines for appeals and so on. There is no provision in Bosnian law preventing a prosecutor from amending the indictment, including other indictees. There were several additional indictees. I think that there were six. Some of them were -- charges were dropped by the Prosecution. And an indictment can be amended to include certain other criminal offences without prior approval of the Trial Chamber, which means that this could lead to undue delay in the conclusion of the trial. This would unnecessarily prolong the proceedings, and with the detention, the fact that the accused would have to stay in detention, this would mean that they would have to wait for at least a year and a year and a half before the beginning of the trial. There is also the issue of Defence counsel. My learned colleague has touched upon that, but we will just mention it briefly. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to the current legislation, nobody who has not been registered by the relevant bodies in Bosnia and Herzegovina can practice law. There are certain provisions in exceptional circumstances allowing foreign lawyers to practice law there, but unless these provisions apply, only those persons registered in the registry of attorneys at law in Bosnia and Herzegovina can practice law there. When it comes to the issue whether the accused would have a fair trial, if an accused cannot have their Defence counsel of choice and if another Defence counsel has to take on the case, this would mean that this new Defence counsel would have to study the whole record, and it could take again at least a year and a year and a half. As for the budget that was proposed by the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina registry, does not contain any headings, any information about lawyers or Defence counsel. The Prosecution filed a motion -- actually informed us that it would be submitting about 200 kilos of material about mass graves, about a hundred binders in all. The question is whether the accused could indeed be represented by proper Defence counsel, or whether the appointment of new Defence counsel would again mean undue delay in their trial. We believe that it would. We also have another issue, which is hearing witnesses, and whether both the Prosecution and the Defence would be able to call witnesses under equal conditions. The Bosnia and Herzegovina law is very restrictive, particularly in light of the provisions according to which the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina can take judicial notice of adjudicated facts and findings, in particular because we have a decision in this case by the Presiding Judge Robinson indicating that only the historical context before World War II can be considered as stipulated -- that can be stipulated. Furthermore, it would be very difficult to call witnesses to Bosnia and Herzegovina because Bosnia and Herzegovina does not have the instrument of safe conduct. The chief prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina indicated that there would be a large number of new indictments, covering about 10.000 people. And in light of the fact that the Office of the Prosecutor has already interviewed many witnesses in this case and in view of the fact that many of them have been characterised as suspects, it would indeed be very difficult to call those witnesses to come to testify in Sarajevo if that were the venue for the trial. The people would not feel safe and witnesses simply do not believe that protective measures would indeed be applied properly. All the Defence counsel agree that the Trial Chamber should be satisfied that conditions for a fair trial would be met, and then and only then would we be able to even consider whether other conditions for the referral of the case under Rule 11 bis were met. And I hope that my colleagues from Bosnia and Herzegovina will not take it personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, before we continue I would have one short question to you. utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps could you assist, Mr. Usher?

utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to apologise, Your Honour. Now I can hear you but before I did not receive any interpretation.

utterances.text: Okay. The matter has been resolved. Mr. Simic, I had one very short question to you. utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct, Your Honour. You are correct that the pre-trial detention is one year, but from the transfer of the accused to Sarajevo, from that date for one year, according to the Bosnia and Herzegovina laws. So from the date of the transfer of the accused, if I am -- if my information is correct, so the detention could last for one year from the date of the transfer of the accused.

utterances.text: Is my information correct that it was six months pre-trial detention and that a judgement then would have to be delivered within one year, which is different from what you tell us. utterances.text: If you have one second, please.

utterances.text: Ms. Nedic, I think you would like to address us, or if you have passed the message meanwhile to Mr. Simic we could hear from him as well, but if you want to address the Court, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wish to say, Your Honours, is that in fact it's a maximum of six months in investigation, in view of the gravity of the crime, and a year from the time the indictment is confirmed to the trial judgement. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he referred to one year and a half someone would have to stay in detention until the start of the trial, which is of course a different thing. The next aspect to be dealt with by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next aspect we should touch upon is mentioned in paragraph 2 of the OTP further submission filed 21st February of 2005. And it's actually the issue of re-extradition or U-turn, as I heard it's popularly called here in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a few documents here I will rely on. If necessary, we can copy them, maybe before tomorrow, but they are all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accessible on the Internet so I think not only you can find it but I am sure Your Honours are already aware of them because some issues have been raised in some other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As it was mentioned before, all four accused voluntarily surrendered to this Tribunal, two of them coming from Serbia and Montenegro, or Yugoslavia at that time; one surrendered directly to the UN and one surrendered, although living in Serbia and Montenegro at that time, surrendered to the authorities of Republika Srpska, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Today the Prosecution mentioned that citizenship should not be concerned of this Tribunal, and it said on page 8, line 13, and we are of a completely opposite opinion on this side of the courtroom. The suggested re-transfer or re-extradition to Bosnia and Herzegovina would hopefully be opposed by the Government of Serbia and Montenegro, and we'll probably hear about it from them, and it would contravene the long-standing customary international law that requires the consent of the transferring state before a person can be re-transferred to another state. One of the examples we have dealing with this issue is a model treaty on extradition by the General Assembly, Resolution 45/116 from 14th December, 1990. In its Article 14 this model treaty on extradition says "A person extradited shall not be re-extradited to a third state, other than then, under B, in respect of which the request of which the requested state consents." We know that transfer of the accused to the ICTY is not considered as a genuine extradition, but we'll deal with that issue later on, and we think that still the rules of re-extradition still apply in this case. Our position, humble position, is that this is a universally accepted principle in this area of the international law. We have a lot of two-party treaties as an example for this matter as well. But I would like to draw your attention to the European Convention on Extradition from the 13th of December, 1957. In its Article 15, this convention says: "The requesting party shall not, without the consent of the requested party, surrender to another party or to a third state a person surrendered to the requesting party." So we think that this convention is of the same standpoint as the General Assembly's model treaty on extradition. Even the rules of the Tribunal, this Tribunal, ICTY, prescribe only transfer to the Tribunal, not from the Tribunal. We have Rule 68(B) of the Rules and Article 29 of the Statute, and they deal with this issue. I would move on, with your permission, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Rules against re-transfer or re-extradition without consent of the transferring state to persons surrendered to international tribunals is established by treaties entered into by the United States with India, Sri Lanka, United Kingdom, South Africa. A typical provision provides: "Where a person has been surrendered to the requesting state by the requested state, the requesting state shall not surrender that person to any third state or an international tribunal unless the requested state consents." This Tribunal has to have in mind that it is creating the international law that could be applied to the USA tomorrow, to the United States of America and their treaties. The constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at that time, or Serbia and Montenegro today, in its Article 17 provides: "A Yugoslav citizen cannot be stripped of its citizenship, cannot be deported from the country, and cannot be extradited to another country." This is common practice in many constitutions of the civil law countries; that it forbids extradition to another country of its own citizens. And our humble opinion is that the extradition to another state would undermine the rationale used by the Tribunal to encourage states as Serbia and Montenegro to surrender its own citizens to this Tribunal. And it's our opinion also that it would breach a faith of the Serbia and Montenegro to this Tribunal and could cause problems in the future when dealing with voluntarily surrendering or arresting and surrendering of the citizens of Serbia and Montenegro to this Tribunal. My learned friend Simic already mentioned a connection between a fair trial and re-extradition, and I would like to address this issue of a fair trial now. And a fair trial is something that is prescribed even by the Rule 11 bis, the rule of the -- of this Tribunal, which says, for the record: "The Referral Bench may order such referral proprio motu or at the request of the Prosecutor after having given to the Prosecutor and, where applicable, the Defence, the accused, the opportunity to be heard and -- and -- after being satisfied that the accused will receive a fair trial." It is frequently recognised by the international and international [sic] settings that trials need not be held in the places where the crimes were allegedly committed, especially when the right of an accused to a fair trial is involved. We have both international and national examples on this issue. My learned friend Simic already mentioned the creation of ICTR, International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. In his report from the 13th February, 1995, The Secretary-General, in paragraph 42, states: "Although the international character of the Rwanda Tribunal is a guarantee of a just and fair conduct of the legal process, it is nevertheless necessary to ensure not only the reality but also the appearance or complete impartiality and objectivity in the Prosecution of persons responsible for crimes committed by both sides to the conflict. Justice and fairness, therefore, require the trial proceedings be held in a neutral territory." As I mentioned, this is said by the Secretary-General of the United States. We understand that -- what did I say -- the United Nations, sorry. We understand the issue of a closing strategy of this Tribunal, but as this Defence already mentioned, it cannot be the most important issue in this hearing. My learned friend also mentioned the Lockerbie trial of two Lebanese, and on that issue we have a document issued by the UN, by the Security Council of the United Nations by the number of S1998/794 of the 27th of August, 1998, where it also welcomes joint United Kingdom/United States initiative and Netherlands willingness to try Arabian airline bombing suspects on the neutral territory. Beside these international examples, we have also national examples, meaning examples from the national jurisdiction where it is provided that, because of the serious issues, the trial can be transferred from one region of the same state to another region of the same state. For example - and we find this one because it's always easy to find the US laws on the Internet - the federal rules of criminal proceedings of the United States of America in its rule 21, prescribe for prejudice: "Upon the defendant's motion, the Court must transfer the proceeding against the defendant to another district if the Court is satisfied that so great a prejudice against the defendant exists in the transferring district that the defendant cannot obtain a fair and impartial trial there." And (B): "For convenience, upon the defendant's motion, the Court may transfer the proceeding or one or more counts against the defendant to another district for the convenience of the parties and witnesses and in the interest of justice." And the last but not the least, Bosnian legislation. Concretely, the criminal proceedings court for the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina also contains a section for change of venue from place where the crime was committed, "if important grounds exists," quote, and it's in Article 3(5). So it's our position that if -- that this case cannot be transferred or re-extradited to another case, Bosnia and Herzegovina firstly, without the consent of Serbia and Montenegro. And if the same is done, these accused cannot expect a fair trial in front of any court in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just put one question to you, Mr. Lukic. You promised us that you would explain to us why a surrender to the Tribunal would be the same as an extradition, because you heavily relied upon many, many treaty provisions, saying that re-extradition is only permitted under certain conditions such as consent by the state or lapse of a certain period of time or -- but do you have any authority for what you seem to put on an equal level as well, that if someone turns themselves in voluntarily, if he's not surrendered by state force, which is of course one of the -- I would say one of the vital characteristics of extradition, if I'm living in Germany and if Belgium is asking my extradition, even if I know that I could be arrested the next day if I say, no, I have to stand trial in Belgium so I'll go to Belgium and I'm not going to wait until I'm arrested, until the moment by force and perhaps after court proceedings was sent to Belgium, do you have any authority where the re-extradition clause would apply if there has been no formal extradition?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I said, although we know that the transfer to the Tribunal is not formally recognised as the extradition, we made many similar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. The transfer to the Tribunal, I understand that you are sent there by force of a state, a state which is under an obligation for the Tribunal that would be under chapter 7 of the United Nations Charter and on the basis of Article 29 of our Statute is under an obligation to arrest whoever the Tribunal asked to be arrested and to send that person. I tend to agree with you that one of the major characteristics for extradition, that is the use of the force by a state that sent someone to another jurisdiction in order to be tried or in order to serve his sentence would come quite close to an extradition, even if it bears a different name. But if you would expect to be arrested, if you would expect that whether under treaty obligations or whether under Chapter 7 of the United Nations' Charter, if you would expect that once arrested you will be sent and if at that moment you say, Well, I'll turn myself in, I'll travel to The Hague and I came voluntarily, because that's part of your position as well, would that also be the same as an extradition?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how much you are familiar with that voluntary surrendering of the people, the accused, but that -- at one moment the investigator put the hand on their shoulder and said, From now on you are arrested. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the difference is often invoked in sentencing hearings --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we hear from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One addition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They all have been put into detention by Yugoslavia. Whoever voluntarily surrenders, he's put into detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We are perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there is a formal decision on that for every and each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you actually say, it's not that voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's voluntarily up to the authorities of the state. From then on, they cannot play games with it anymore, they have to put them into detention and transfer them to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who's next to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will deal with the gravity of the crimes charged against Zeljko Mejakic and also his rank, as both of these elements are essential for the evaluation of the motion for referral. In our view, we need to start from Article 15 -- or rather, Count 15 of the consolidated indictment, according to which beatings and other murders and other forms of mistreatment, including sexual assaults, were usual in the Omarska camp; that the guards and the visitors who frequently came to the camp used all kinds of weapons and implements -- instruments to beat and otherwise physically abuse the detainees. According to this paragraph of the indictment, hundreds of detainees, known and unknown, did not survive. Therefore, the first question that arises is whether such acts represent a serious crime, of course provided that the allegations are true - however, at present we are simply considering the counts in the indictment - and whether they justify extradition, or rather, a referral under Rule 11 bis (C). I will also respond to the position of the Prosecutor. My learned friend has said these are very grave crimes which are alleged in the indictment, but that they can still be referred under Rule 11 bis. In our view, this is a contradiction. If these crimes are so serious, they cannot fall within the category of crimes which justify a referral under Rule 11 bis (C). The Defence wishes to remind Your Honours of the fact that many of the accused before this Tribunal who were lower-ranking were tried before this Tribunal. We also have paragraph 24 of the indictment in which the rank of Zeljko Mejakic is described. He is said to be the camp commander of the Omarska camp and that he had effective control over the guard shift commanders, camp guards, and other persons working within or frequently visiting the Omarska camp. There is also a confidential part of the indictment which I will not discuss here, but in general terms it is alleged that many of these visitors and guards committed the crimes alleged against Zeljko Mejakic under Article 7(1) and (3) of the Statute of this Tribunal, the article that deals with command responsibility. A further question which arises is whether a camp commander who has control over all persons employed in the camp or visiting the camp where, as the indictment alleges, hundreds of people were murdered and several thousand people tortured and illegally detained, whether this can be a medium-rank person according to the Prosecution's submission of the 21st of February of this year. If it is correct that all these crimes were committed in the camp and there was a camp commander who had control over all the perpetrators of such crimes, he can by no means be described as a person of medium significance. We feel that the Prosecution view has been adapted to suit the requirements of Rule 11 bis. Therefore, in our view, the conditions in Rule 11 bis (C) have not been met and we move that the Court reject them. Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Next, I would like to finish in approximately 10 minutes from now. I take it that you'll be able to finish, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We ought to. I'll try to just highlight and develop some points, may it please the Court. Dan Ivetic, appearing on behalf of Dusan Fustar, but my comments here today will also apply to the joint Defence filings that have been filed and responses that we have prepared to certain items that the Prosecution has raised. I will also try to save time for Ms. Nedic since she has very important points that I would ask this trial to consider that she is going to present to you. The first point that I would like to discuss and raise is in response to my learned colleague from the Office of the Prosecution's suggestion that this case is appropriate for Rule 11 bis and implying that Rule 11 bis -- that this case is ideal for Rule 11 bis. What has to be taken into account and has been alluded to previously by my colleagues is the fact that three of the accused that are presently before this Tribunal and before the Trial Chamber surrendered themselves in the year 2002. Specifically, my client, Mr. Fustar, surrendered himself on January 31st of 2002. Mr. Gruban, thereafter, I believe turned himself on May the 2nd, 2002; and shortly thereafter Mr. Knezevic also turned himself in voluntarily on May the 18th of 2002. Significantly, this is all prior to the amendment of Rule 11 bis, which for the first time created the notion that a case could be deferred to a national court. At the time that these individuals submitted themselves to the Tribunal and at the time that proceedings were at that time proceeding against them, the version of Rule 11 bis that existed provides merely for a suspension of the Tribunal's indictment in the case if the state that arrested the accused already had proceedings underway and was willing and able to proceed with that case. In that circumstance, the Trial Chamber would have the opportunity to suspend the ICTY indictment until those proceedings were completed. Now, what is critical is that it is respectfully submitted that the purpose of the rule at that point in time was economy of resources, not to have the Tribunal duplicate a proceeding that was already prepared, already underway, and since the entity that was to do this proceeding had the individual and had arrested him, it would be more efficient for them to proceed with the proceedings. But that is not the case with the new Rule 11, which implies a certain different set of circumstances. Now, the rules of the ICTY stipulate, in particular Rule 6, that any time an amendment -- any time a Rule is amended, that amendment shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused or of a convicted or acquitted person in any pending case. It is respectfully submitted that at the time that Rule 11 bis was amended in 2002, after the surrender of three of the accused here, there was definitely proceedings pending in the ICTY and Rule 6(D) did apply to prevent that amendment from gravely impacting and prejudicing the accused. The application of the current Rule 11 to this case would therefore be improper for several reasons. One of the reasons, which I will not go into great detail since we have presented very detailed arguments and facts in our varied submissions, both the joint submissions and the separate submissions by counsel for Mr. Mejakic, my learned colleague Mr. Simic, that's one reason why the new Rule 11 bis shall not apply. Another reason is, particularly for my client, that the old Rule 11 bis, which should be effective as to him, indicates that this type of suspension of the indictment would occur where another state actually arrested him. That's not the case for Mr. Fustar. Mr. Fustar was never arrested by the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina or any other state, for that matter. We submitted ourselves directly to the United Nations after having private and direct discussions with the Tribunal and the Office of the Prosecutor to effectuate that request. He submitted himself directly to the United Nations personnel and was arrested by the United Nations personnel. There was not a single Bosnian governmental authority present. So therefore, under the old Rule 11 bis that should still apply to him by operation of Rule 6(D), this case is not appropriate for deferral under the new Rule 11 bis. The second issue I would like to just highlight and develop is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with respect to witness protection issues in the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the Office of the Prosecutor has proposed that this case should be referred. My learned colleague has alluded to the fact that this state court as far as we know, since we have not received any official response from the state court, we have not received any official information either to the request that we made back in September of 2004 or to the request that the learned Trial Chamber has made of the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we have not heard their responses; we don't know what their position is.
