utterances.text: I apologise. A correction. I am trying to present information that my colleagues prepared on that respect. The problem is that many of the witnesses do not want to testify via videolink and therefore that device cannot be used to remedy the problem of witnesses coming to Sarajevo. There is another group of witnesses that would have difficulty coming to Sarajevo, and those are Bosniak Muslim witnesses. They fear that if they come to testify in support of ethnic Serb defendants, that they will be accosted, that their families will receive pressure from the areas that they live in which are predominantly ethnic Muslim locations. The third category of witnesses that would have difficulty under the Defence in Sarajevo would be individuals who fear that they might be arrested and further indicted. We've already from my colleague Mr. Simic that the public prosecutor in Bosnia and Herzegovina has boasted that as many as 10.000 new defendants will be arrested, will be indicted, will be tried. That has inflamed the public and people are frightful that they don't know who is going to be subject to arrest, trial, and prosecution. Not only do we have regular citizens who are fearful that they will be wrongfully arrested, but we have individuals who were involved in the activities in Keraterm, in Omarska, in the police, in the military, in Prijedor, who would be vital Defence witnesses and some of whom were the subject of indictments before the ICTY that were withdrawn with the caveat that national courts could still indict these individuals. They obviously would not come to Sarajevo to testify for fear of being arrested and indicted and therefore the Defence could likely be left with no actual witnesses to present at that point in time. The last point that I would like to raise is in response to the Prosecution's representation that the anonymity problem has been resolved. It is our understanding based upon the research and the material that was provided to the Defence that Articles 13 through 22, 19, and 21 of the law on protection of witnesses under threat and vulnerable witnesses still provide for very drastic proceedings in which a witness who is -- who is sensible -- sensitive to a particular defendant or to a particular set of facts can be allowed to testify not only outside of the presence of the defendant, but also outside of the presence of the Defence counsel. It is our understanding that there are provisions that would be employed in Sarajevo that such witnesses could give testimony only to the Court, in private session, and that their information as to who these witnesses are would be kept confidential for in upwards of 30 years, making it very unlikely and impossible for the Defence to prepare rebuttal evidence and rebuttal testimony with respect to these witnesses. That is a very serious due process problem with the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And again, if we can get more -- if we can get access to the submissions from the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we can verify whether in fact this information is accurate, but that is the result of our research into this matter, that those articles exist and create a difficulty for obtaining due process and justice were this case to be transferred. Now I would defer to my colleague Ms. Nedic for her submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps, because you have our own interpretation of what two or three minutes are, I would limit Ms. Nedic too much if I would invite her to make further submissions now. Perhaps we first have a break -- we'll have a break until 5.00. And if at any later stage, Mr. Ivetic, you could pay attention to -- well, international case law on anonymous witnesses because you have described the issue as a human rights concern. I'm not saying I'm disagreeing with you, but I would like to deepen out a bit the problem in the light of the international case law on anonymous witnesses. That certainly would assist the Chamber. We adjourn until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Nedic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I wanted to talk about is the application of the laws that might be applicable to the accused in this case. I would like to refer first of all to the arguments provided by the Prosecution in its brief of the 21st of February that we have not been able to understand fully. In paragraphs 14 and 15 -- in paragraph 14 it says that practically all the provisions of the law of the Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the international law are the same, and it further says in paragraph 15 that the Criminal Code of SFRY contains no provisions which would refer to crimes against humanity or command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Nedic, could I invite you to slow down a bit for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I don't know if the Prosecution has made it uncontestable that the SFRY Criminal Code was in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. If that is the case, we would not be forced to provide any arguments in that matter, but I expect the Prosecution to make its views plain. In view of their submissions in their brief, it would seem so. I would like to stress that first of all it is not correct that the Criminal Code of the SFRY does not contain provisions against crimes against humanity and command responsibility. Quite the contrary. There is a whole chapter, Chapter 16, and Articles from 141 through 156 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, which deal precisely with those offences, crimes against humanity and against humanitarian law. Article 142 might perhaps be the one that might apply because it is entitled "crimes against the civilian population." That would seem so at first sight. I would like to stress that in fact the law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not contain any provisions relating to war crimes. War crimes were defined and sanctioned in the federal law because the federal state deemed that issue to be much too important to be left to the discretion of the republics. And that is why it is only regulated in the federal law. The question is, the Prosecution claims, that in order for the new Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina to apply, that it might apply. We do not agree with that and we submitted some of the arguments in our 22nd of February motion. I would now not repeat all the ways in which you can determine whether -- which law is in fact more lenient towards the perpetrator, and both the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Criminal Code of the SFRY, one has to apply the law that is more lenient towards the perpetrator. So the Prosecution here used only the arguments relating to the punishment, and we wanted to stress that many other aspects need to be taken into account; whether the criminal offence was indeed qualified as such, whether it entailed a certain type of responsibility for the perpetrator, and the final consideration is the punishment itself. But we stress that no offence could be punishable by death penalty as the only penalty prescribed. There always had to be the alternative punishment of imprisonment. The Criminal Code of the SFRY provided for two alternatives to death penalty. First of all, for every criminal offence it was usually stipulated that the perpetrator could either be punished by imprisonment, usually the minimum imprisonment -- length of imprisonment was stipulated, or by death penalty, and there was then a special provision in the Criminal Code of the SFRY which stipulated that the death penalty could be replaced by the term of imprisonment of 20 years. So even if we only look at those provisions that relate to the punishment itself, we could state that the law, the 1992 law, is the law that should apply because it is more lenient. We even found out that there is a decision of the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina expressing the view that the law dating from 1992 is more lenient, that is judgement 208/2 of the 10th of July, 1997, of -- against the accused Osman Hodzic. It is the famous Ristovic case for crimes against Serbs as part of the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So we disagree with the arguments proffered by the Prosecution that the new law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the new Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina would apply. As regards the international law, I have to say that the Criminal Code of the SFRY stipulated in Article 3 that no one can be sentenced in any way or sanctioned in any way for a criminal offence that, before it was committed, was not qualified as a criminal offence and which did not have any penalty attached to it. And Article 211 of the constitution of SFRY contains the same provision. I have to apologise, there is a slight error in the transcript as regards the judgement against Osman Hodzic. It is not dated 1997 but 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have a copy for the Chamber? Perhaps even --

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we will be able to provide you a copy by tomorrow if you agree to give us this deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can't expect you to give it to us right away. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to the death penalty, I would like to note another aspect. The constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, published in the Official Gazette 3/92, abolished the death penalty. So it was in March -- published on the 16th of March, 1992. I also wanted to make a few arguments regarding what the Prosecution said about the Defence counsel that might or might not represent their clients as foreign nationals in proceedings before a court in Sarajevo. According to the law on the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, lawyers can be selected or if they are appointed by the court to indigent accused, they are selected from a list of lawyers of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the court -- the rules of procedure of the court may stipulate any circumstances in which lawyers that are not on the list may be allowed to represent the accused. I have to stress that we tried many times to obtain from the registry of the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to obtain the rules of procedure of that court and in order to be able to determine whether there are any conditions under which we might continue to represent our clients in Sarajevo and whether indeed we meet those conditions, and we have yet to receive the rules of procedure. I don't know why, whether it indeed exists, whether those stipulate -- those provisions about the Defence counsel exist. The representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina should actually make their views clear on that. I would also like to say something briefly about the law on protection of witnesses, which is currently in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The amendments thereto were passed on the 29th of December, 2004, and were published in the Official Gazette 61, number 61. But we compared the existing text with the amendments and we were unable to find Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any significant amendments. We believe that they're mostly linguistic in character and that all our objections made with regard to this law, particularly Articles 15 through 22, that make it possible for a protected witness to be questioned without the presence of the parties so that this witness be questioned just by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber, the Judges, then read the statements at the trial, the Judges then ask the parties whether they want to ask any additional questions, and if the parties say no, then the Judges decide whether -- whether the witness would be heard again and whether any questions might be -- additional questions by the party may be put to this witness, thus eliminating any cross-examination of the witness. And since the Defence is unable to determine the identity of the witness for 30 years after the finality of the judgement, there is no possibility for the Defence to avail itself of the extraordinary legal remedies available to it and to present any new facts or circumstances that arise in regard -- or that are related to this protected witness. The law on protection of witnesses in Article 13 also stipulates that the identity of the witness must be disclosed to the other party at the trial at the latest. We believe that this is too late because in that case the Defence really is unable to question the credibility of the witness or to obtain any evidence that would stand to impeach the witness. In its brief, the Prosecution noted that the identity of all the witnesses is already known to the Defence and it has been made known to them in the course of the pre-trial proceedings. But we believe that the prosecution in Bosnia and Herzegovina is not bound in any way to stick to this witness list and nothing prevents them from calling additional witnesses. So that we believe that this does not in fact answer to our question. This is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nedic. I was informed, Ms. Somers, that you would like to briefly respond -- as a matter of fact, we might have some questions as well and I'm considering what would be better, that we first hear your response and that perhaps we ask for some clarifications and that we then give an opportunity to the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia and Montenegro to give their views, because we have received them in writing, and I reluctantly have to inform the Defence that the filing of last Friday, which was quite voluminous, has been sent to you by DHL one of these days, yesterday perhaps. So this was, at least in the view of the Chamber, not the most efficient way of giving you the information that is contained in these submissions. We apologise for that, but I suggest that the Defence will have an opportunity to make further submissions in writing based on the material and the views as expressed by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the many, many legal texts attached to it. We'll set -- perhaps you first read it and then you'll hear how much you would get for it. Perhaps, Ms. Somers, I heard that you'd like to briefly respond. Perhaps one of the -- one, I emphasise -- one of the issues seems to be the applicable law. There are different views on that. Perhaps you could include that if you respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Some of my comments may require further comment, depending on what our esteemed representatives say as well, but from the standpoint of what was said by my learned colleagues from the Defence, I'd like to point out that they have presented a very logical reason: This is a ready-for-trial case that has arguably more jurisprudence at the hand of the general public as well as the Defence than any other case in the Tribunal upon which to familiarise themselves for a speedy trial, speedy in the sense of expeditious, without any untoward delay. It is currently a case that has more adjudicated facts at the disposal of all counsel and of the Bench than probably any other set of facts in the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand the Defence properly, that referring to the decision of Judge Robinson, that there was only limited material that could be accepted as adjudicated facts? Perhaps the situation might have changed since a couple of days. I can imagine that. But I remember that a different position was taken as far as adjudicated facts are concerned. Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am speaking on behalf of all the Defence counsel. Judge Robinson's Chamber issued a decision limiting the facts to a very limited number of facts up to World War II as indisputable because there were very many different facts presented in the various trials concerning Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. That was in my mind, so I was a bit surprised, Ms. Somers, when I heard you say that this was a case --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't think, Your Honour, that it's a terribly limiting decision by His Honour Judge Robinson. In fact, just to let the Chamber know, the decision is -- I believe at April -- 1st of April, 2004, and it cites, just for clarity for the record: "Hereby admits the following facts, 1 through 72, 74, 105, 111 through 120, et cetera, et cetera, and this covers a span well beyond the World War II period up to various facts -- up to various facts in 1992. So I think that although it was not all-inclusive, it certainly does not cover the pre-World War II period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have some expertise on this Bench in -- on the matter and it's all public decisions --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We won't pursue that anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Not at all. The -- there is law. I regret that my learned colleagues opposite have not had a chance to see the law, but the acceptance of adjudicated facts and a decision of law is set forth in Article 4 of the law on transfer of cases, and I would just ask that when an opportunity is -- presents itself, to take a look at it, but in fact the binding decisions in the course of the ICTY are naturally to be taken into account, but it specifies it and I think it's helpful to the Chamber. On the issue of -- I almost have to paraphrase it -- "If we had known that this change was going to occur, we would never have surrendered." I find this an absolutely invalid, almost offensive, assertion. The duty to present one's self to the Tribunal when indicted exists. It is not conditional, it is not a contract with the Tribunal, it is a duty. And the suggestion that "had we known..." As it is, one of the reasons, and I know this is so obvious I only have to state it for the record, that we have this breakup of hearings is because people serially, at their own convenience or at the convenience of other perhaps undisclosed persons surrender or present themselves to this Tribunal rather than allowing the proper or the all-in-one hearing. Yes, there have been a number of cases in which these facts have been the subject of prosecutions. It is not in the main because they could not have been tried at once; it was a decision consciously made by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Again, this case -- and we have no reason to assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, I just -- I hope you don't mind if I try -- if I'm seeking clarification. You say it's the duty to present one's self to the Tribunal. I am aware of the duty of states to surrender accused to the Tribunal. I am not aware of a duty at this moment, and I checked with my colleagues how this would be in their domestic systems, that there is a duty, perhaps apart from a kind of a moral duty, but if I am aware that I have to stand trial and I just decide not to appear, is there a legal duty to come? And where do we find the basis for that duty?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Perhaps I should recast the observation and suggest that once the fact of indictment is known to an accused one can obviously elude presentation to the relevant Tribunal as long as one can get away with it, but the fact is the indictment exists and, yes, there is a state duty, based on Article 29, and in fact harbouring or allowing the evasion of fulfilling that duty by permitting the person to remain on the territory has other ramifications, and I would leave that as the other parameter for this argument. But the suggestion that "I wouldn't have done it but for ..." given the very special nature of how we came into existence as a body and that same body that put us into existence has mandated that we take those serious cases -- and I repeat that by virtue of our title, this is a Tribunal for prosecution of violations of serious international humanitarian law, there's no question that everything that's here is a serious violation. So the suggestion that we have a deal to be struck I think is not correct. And then the suggestion that the gravity is really -- that there are various degrees of gravity, well, of course. But to be here in the first place it has to be a grave or serious violation of international humanitarian law. I want to put that to one side because I see that interwoven on a regular basis in argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I nevertheless ask you a question because you say -- but the suggestion, you said "I wouldn't have done it but for..." isn't the argument "I did it but you changed what I did."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "I presented myself to the Tribunal and suddenly I'm not standing before the Tribunal anymore but before another court. And what I did was unconditional. Apart from that, it would have the same meaning, that it would be the same as what I did." If I voluntarily go to the army and end up in -- I'm voluntarily ascribing to the army and I suddenly end up in a metal factory -- well, I wanted to go to the army, not anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This Tribunal has been granted the authority to make the referrals, and as part of that authority, however the accused ends up here, he or she is also subject to what changes come on -- come along as a result of the enforcement of the mandate by the Security Council. There is -- I understand it's a grey area, but it is not, in our view, a pure -- an extradition question. It is a question of the powers that are inherent in carrying out the mandate of the Security Council under Chapter 7, and any changes that have to be effected in order to continue to carry it out, which include, perhaps unfortunately, but the need to pare down to only those very, very high-level cases, given its finite status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, could you respond to one of the issues raised by Mr. Ivetic in relation to possible application of Rule 6(D).

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As to the prejudice, Your Honour, the possibility of prejudice which result in rule changes. Is that what Your Honour is referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You raised that in your submission of the 21st of February. You said that -- it's page -- "There's no evidence that the rights of the accused will be prejudiced or that the state court will be less reliable and exhibit less due process guarantees than the ICTY." Could you elaborate on that, responding to the submission of Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no proof or any evidence that has been submitted of a systemic problem with this new state court. In fact, this body perhaps offers more safeguards than would have been contemplated because of, A, the international character, A [sic], the international interest, deep interest in making sure that matters which, for example, come to it from us, from this body, are carried out with all the necessary due process safeguards. There is not anything that has been suggested, other than innuendo based on other comments about allegations of government persons, that it cannot work. In fact, it's been untested in that respect. And in the absence of some suggestion of a systemic fault so deep, which seems very unlikely, I think that that is a baseless suggestion by counsel. I believe it was without merit. Now, may I proceed into a question that His Honour Judge Orie also asked me to ask about the law. It is not always going to be possible to have identical charges; it may not work. We are going into national jurisdictions. Comparable charges with due process guarantees that meet the requirements that have been laid out are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll go into the substantive law later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you stay in rules in relation to 6(D) a little further. In your submission here you compared two scenarios, one being the situation of the accused being tried in the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the other being the situation of the accused being tried at the ICTY. However, speaking for myself, the comparison should be between the trial in Serbia and Montenegro and the trial in the court of BiH. The reason is because of the -- sort of retroactive application of Rule 11 bis. 11 bis was enacted in 1997 and at that time the only referral envisaged by that original rule was the referral to the state where the accused was arrested. So of course there is an issue whether the arrest and voluntary surrender are two different matters. But if we set aside that issue for the moment and if we presuppose -- just suppose that every aspect or conditions of the two nations' legal systems in terms of fairness or due process of law are the same, then would there not be a possibility of viewing the trial in the court of BiH less favourable to the accused than that in Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I am not sure on which particular grounds His Honour thinks that it might be less favourable, but I think from the standpoint of two equal courts only for the sake of argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Might it not be a general conception that everybody would prefer to be tried in his homeland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes, Your Honour. Depending on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would be your observation on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That it is not only where one prefers, that is a kind of, as His Honour knows, forum shopping. If in fact where the crimes are committed, and if one looks at the setting out, the stacking as it were, in 11 bis, if any significance is attached to it, it places the place where the crimes are committed as the first. It's not -- I submit that it's -- it should have some reason for that, and if all other factors are equal, the place where the crimes are committed, in our view, should be the first locus where possible. I am unable to analyse the similarities or dissimilarities between the Serbia and Montenegro system because I don't have as much information on it here, but I think that there is a rational basis for having the place of -- where the crimes were committed as the first. Again, looking at what is up and running and ready to go in Sarajevo, if this Chamber makes a determination that all aspects of due process are complied with, then there would really be no reason why -- at least, I have not for myself heard anything that would suggest that anything other than a fair trial could be had in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which indeed is a multi-ethnic republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I just -- I'm confident the Chamber has looked at the provisions of Rule 58, but I just want to bring to its attention, of course, again the issue of national extradition, et cetera, et cetera, should extradition become a central point in the Chamber's determination. On the -- although it was addressed earlier, if perhaps my learned counsel opposite feels that the level of the accused is so high as to preclude a transfer or not to be in compliance with the provision of Rule 11 bis, I would have to disagree. In fact, within the scheme of Omarska, let's say as to accused Mejakic, the command -- commander position, the police commander position, albeit at the top of a ladder is not at the top of the ladder and fits well within the group of persons mid-level in the scheme of things who could be heard in a state or local court. As to the -- which law will apply, the complexity of the issue is such that my brief comments will not do very much, I think, to help it, but if it is the court -- if it is referred to the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would be my understanding, subject to correction, that it is that court that will decide which law would apply, unless that is one of factors right now that the Chamber will have to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't have to determine what law the court in Bosnia and Herzegovina would apply, but of course we have to find out what kind of charges could be realistically brought against the accused in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and therefore the applicable law is certainly one of the elements, at least, thoughts on what would be the applicable law, especially since there seems to be quite some disagreement as to whether the BH Criminal Code of 2003 would apply, which gives some reference to international law and where the government has indicated that since in 1992 that -- that the 2003 code mainly qualifies what was already international law in 1992. And that raises, well, at least a couple of questions which I'd very much like you to say at least whatever you can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm -- without really being able to predict how this Chamber would view the -- if the hovering over of principles of customary international law, but not necessarily full incorporation into -- or enabling into, we acknowledge that there are some difficulties, there's some very grey areas. However, there is and has been the provision of crimes against -- war crimes against the civilian population, or I believe it's called war crimes against civilians, that as I referred to earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the Criminal Code of the federal republic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Both then and now. Both then and now. There is a provision called war crimes against civilians. And it embodies a good deal of the type of criminal conduct that goes into let's say crimes against humanity, persecutions, and in the absence of the discriminatory intent and widespread and systematic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, I remember hat Ms. Nedic raised the question of whether that Criminal Code of the federal republic was applicable in BiH at all at the time. Are you in the position to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm not a BH constitutional lawyer, but I believe that the republican level would have looked to the federal level for any type of gap, if I recall from other cases that I've been involved in, but I cannot address that specifically. And if the Chamber has no objection to referring it to the appropriate expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The relation of two Criminal Codes is not very clear to me. Did Serbia and Montenegro have their own Criminal Code at that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask the Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm just not -- couldn't pull it out of my head right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we can hear that from the representative later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask one more question. It's about the command responsibility. Three accused, as far as I understand, they are accused under 7(3). So you must be confident that in Bosnian court -- in the court of BiH, such legal regime should exist, but unfortunately it is not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. clear from your submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It appears that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It appears that there is no strict -- and again I would stand corrected by my colleagues from BiH, no strict equivalent of our 7(3), of the concept of 7(3). There are other provisions which perhaps, if translated, suggest that where duties exist, certain omissions -- or if certain acts are committed and there is a failure to either report it or act on it, it's kind of a backward approach -- not backward but a back-door approach to it. But I have not been able to find the exact equivalent of 7(3), and I think that that is a concession that we have to make. There is a concern, however, that the conduct -- that the language of, for example, the war crimes against civilian population may allow, if very adequate charged, and I think the charging becomes very, very important in terms of the language, the language, in its equivalent comparable provisions, what roles were taken and to show that this is committing the offence, acknowledge that it would take careful draftsmanship of the existing -- reworking it into their own criminal regimen, but I believe it can be done. There is not, Your Honour -- I believe you're correct, there is not a comparable one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any further issues you would like to raise in responding briefly?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just, it was unclear by Mrs. Nedic's comment about no questioning -- no ability to question, I mean almost ruling out cross-examination. I would also ask when the Chamber inquires of our colleagues from the BiH if the type of additional questions that are envisioned in that provision are of the nature of cross-examination. And again, it is not clear -- it's a bit less than clear as laid out in the law. Other than that, there is an opportunity to pose questions to witnesses, albeit protected ones, and perhaps under different circumstances than we are used to here, but the opportunity exists. It may, again, not be an exact parallel to the cross-examinations practices of this Tribunal but may yet serve the same interests of justice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the Defence would also be in a better position to respond to that once they've received the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, forgive the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I was just asked to relate to the Chamber that the SFRY code was taken over by Bosnia and Herzegovina as republican law on the 11th of April, 1992, by -- as found in Official Gazette of BH 211.04 1992. This is what I'm relaying as it has come to me, so I hope it may offer some help. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to hear more detail from the representative later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, because as you may have noticed the Chamber has already put some questions to the parties, although not very extensively, the Defence has asked in a few aspects to treat their response as confidential. Is there any need at this moment to deal with those confidential issues, because we then could consider to go into private session for a while. And I have to ask the Defence -- or to deal with them in open session if confidentiality is not of vital importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no reason for private session. Should there be any need, we will request it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that also -- Ms. Somers, you asked at an earlier stage whether you could respond freely. Is there any intention on your part at this moment to go into any area just to -- I think that would not violate the confidentiality to say it has got something to do with counsel, to do with witness protection. Is there any matter you would like to raise at this moment where you would not be sure you could do it in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I cannot think of any, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's then proceed. Let me see whether we have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not raised by the ongoing debate more or less. Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from Ms. Nedic, who said that -- who pointed out some Article 142 in relation to command responsibility. Could you point out the relevant procedure -- I'm sorry, I beg your pardon -- provision which deals with the command responsibility you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour. "Whosoever violating the rules of international law in time of war, an armed conflict or an occupation, orders that murders, torture, inhumane acts, biological experiments, infliction of severe suffering and injuries, physical integrity or health, deportation or transferral or forcible denationalisation or conversion to another religion, forcing to prostitution or rape be committed against the civilian population by using means of coercion or terror, the taking of hostages, collective punishment, illegal detention in concentration camps, and other illegal kinds of detention, depriving of the right to a fair and impartial trial, forcing to serve in the armed forces of a hostile force, or in its intelligence services or administration, forcing to forced labour --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's enough. So can I take it that you are saying --

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a very long article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- that by adopting the international law that it also adopted the principle of command responsibility? Is that your -- the crux of your submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not absolutely sure that the responsibility actually corresponds to the responsibility as provided for in international law and this law so that the two correspond exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you elaborate a bit more. I don't think I followed in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This article provides punishment for acts and for intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I follow up on that, Ms. Nedic. I'm sorry that you sat with the sense of relief, but I call on you again. That article seemed to be directed to conduct in the nature of ordering all these things, direct exercise of authority by a commander. Is there any provision which deals with the more indirect form of command responsibility, that is, where a commander may be found criminally responsible for the acts of the soldiers under command or responsible because the commander has failed to punish criminal acts by those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite honest, in view of the fact that my defendant has not been charged under Article 7(3), I personally have not gone into the issue of command responsibility in any great depth. I think, however, that the answer is no, but please don't take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that is the issue that was troubling both Judge Kwon and myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I might be able to provide an answer to this question. The form of liability in Article 7(3) of the Statute did not exist in the then-Criminal Code of the SFRY. This indirect form of command responsibility did not exist. As far as I know, although I would have to check this, there was responsibility for directly issuing such an order, and it referred to military commanders. I think it is found in the chapter referring to crimes against the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would there not be a possibility of direct application of internationally accepted law, international treaties?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the then-law of the SFRY, there was no possibility of directly applying the provisions of international law to cases tried pursuant to this law. And that is why we felt that this law was more lenient toward the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And can I ask one more brief question to Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a very hypothetical question, to Mr. Ivetic. Can I hear from you a comment on the submission of the Serbia and Montenegro, or hypothetically, would your client agree or oppose -- the transfer to Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Assuming under the hypothetical that a decision is made for referring the case outward to either Serbia and Montenegro, the -- we believe Serbia and Montenegro would be the better of the two choices, although obviously we believe staying at the Tribunal would be the best choice of all for the reasons that we specified in the various filings that we made, in the hypothetical sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simic, I have a similar question for you. I did understand from the submission by the Government of Serbia and Montenegro that -- I think it was you or Mr. Zivanovic addressed the government with a request to apply for referral of the case to Serbia and Montenegro. Apart from whether that's the proper way of getting a state involved, but could you explain to me if you are saying that the case is not a referable case why you apply to another government to get the case referred?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I have been misunderstood. I informed the government of my country that in the proceedings before the Tribunal, its citizens accused of war crimes might be referred to another country and be tried there. Knowing the situation in the entire region, I felt certain and I feel even more certain today that the most credible judgements that might lead to true reconciliation are only the judgements made by the people of the country whose citizen the accused is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you want to explain the thoughts you had. What I read in the submission by Serbia and Montenegro - and I take it that you have received a copy of that as well - it reads as follows: "On the 14th of December, Mr. Jovan Simic, and Mr. Branko Lukic, the Defence counsel for --" and then they list the accused -- "wrote to the National Council of Serbia and Montenegro for cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and requested that Serbia and Montenegro address the Tribunal and request that the case of Prosecutor versus Mejakic and others be referred to the additional authorities of Serbia and Montenegro, pursuant to Rule 11 bis." I never heard any protest of you against this -- well, this language. It does not say what you just explained to me, but which says Mr. Simic asked us to apply for referral of the case. And of course my question comes from your position in this court that it's a non-referable case and this at least suggests that you sought referral, but then to another state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will repeat: I applied to the National Council in order to inform them that proceedings were being held here under Rule 11 bis. The Defence has no right to request a country to move the Tribunal to have a case referred to a national jurisdiction. The Defence simply wished to inform the government so the government could take steps in favour of its citizens. And in the case of citizens who have voluntarily surrendered, it would be best for them to return to their country. As Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see is that there's a clear disagreement on whether you applied for a referral to be initiated by Serbia and Montenegro or whether you just said, Well, there happens something which might not be good for your citizens, so if you want to do anything, do it, which is of course a different matter, especially in view of the position you take here whether this is a referable case, yes or no. We'll hear from Serbia and Montenegro later, I take it, on this disagreement. I have another question which comes back to the applicable law. It has been invoked by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina provides that Articles 3 and 4 of this code shall not prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which at the time when it was committed was criminal according to the general principles of international law. I am aware that -- I am aware that you have not seen these submissions by the BH government, but if any of the Defence counsel could give me an answer to the question whether such a rule in existence would make it possible to apply customary law which was not codified at the time when a crime was committed, if any of you could comment on that issue, then I'd like to hear from you. Yes, Ms. Nedic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I read these pieces of legislation, Your Honours, I concluded that they're quite contradictory. To be quite frank, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia we had the codified laws, which meant that in criminal law the norms were quite specific; the definition of the criminal offence, the mode of liability of the perpetrator, and the sanctions envisaged for such crimes. And it was impossible to define them in any other way, apart from that in the law. The law in Bosnia and Herzegovina copied to a certain extent the provisions in the SFRY codes and then there were some other provisions added to it which in fact violated the unity of the code itself. In Article 3, which is entitled "The principle of legality," paragraph 1 reads: "Criminal offences and criminal sanctions can be prescribed only by law." Paragraph 2 reads -- is a modification of that, is in contradiction with paragraph 1: "No one can be sentenced or sanctioned in any way for any criminal offence that was not stipulated as such or qualified as a criminal offence, either by domestic or international law before the commission and which did not have a sanction prescribed for it by the law." So these two paragraphs are contradictory because one stipulates that only a law can prescribe crimes and sanctions, whereas the paragraph 2 stipulates that international law can apply here, too, and only sanctions prescribed by law can apply also to that other case. So how this will be applied in practice, how you can decide which sanction to apply, whether you would seek the analogous crime, the one that is most similar, that is qualified in the law, and then to compare it with the international law and to prescribe this same sentence, I think that this is quite illogical in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course sometimes one rule makes an exception to another one and that is, of course, to some extent always in contradiction, but I do understand you say the strict application of the rule of non redric [phoen] that the lex scripta means that there should be a written law which criminalises should be applied and there's contradiction between that exception which is unclear. At the same time, of course, the rule says this -- I just read the text to you, that the foregoing rules would not prevent from ... That means to that extent of course an exception is made, which makes it less contradictory. I would like now, if there are no further questions at this moment, I would like to give an opportunity -- we are limited in our time. We started late due to the snow conditions. I can imagine that if you come from the Serbia or from Bosnia that you laugh a bit about our 15 or 20 centimetres of snow and see that they cause us so many difficulties, but that's our reality at this moment. I'd first like to give an opportunity. We have -- we'll continue tomorrow. Of course we are a bit beyond schedule. We have some -- until the tape ends, we will have presumably until quarter to 7.00, that would be close to half an hour. Of course the Bosnia and Herzegovina is a party in this proceeding, so I would like to give them the floor first and at the same time invite them to keep an eye on the clock so that their neighbours still have time left as well to address the Tribunal. I take it, Madam Kreso, that you can take the floor. You might be more used to being addressed as "Your Honour," but that might be a bit confusing in this court. So, Madam President, may I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for making it possible for the delegation from my state to present the arguments why we deem that we are ready and committed to take on the cases such as the one that is debated here today, to try them in conditions that would ensure a fair trial, and to have trials that will be a result of all the changes that the legal system in Bosnia and Herzegovina has undergone. I could really not accept the argument that financial and political reasons argue in favour of transferring those cases to domestic courts, because we would not accept such reasons. We are experts, professionals, we cannot accept such an argument. This cannot be a reason for a case to be accepted. Let me present in brief what the judiciary of Bosnia and Herzegovina has done in order to equip itself to deal with such sensitive cases. After the war, the judiciary in Bosnia and Herzegovina underwent momentous changes. In the region, in the former Yugoslavia, in fact it has gone furthest in the reform that it underwent. First of all, the appointment of judges and prosecutors is done in a totally different way. No political party, no NGO, nobody except for the high judiciary council appoints the judges, and equal representation of all ethnic groups is complied with from both entities. Members of the high judicial council are our colleagues; defence counsel, prosecutors, judges, all highly respected, professors from the law school, and so on. Our judiciary has incorporated an international element recently. We have international judges and international prosecutors working in our courts. Furthermore, our legislation has been changed and adapted to the international and European standards, and despite the fact that we do have a very rich tradition because we were part of the legal system of the former Yugoslavia, which was itself based on the German law due to the fact that Austria Hungary was present in Bosnia and Herzegovina, after the war, we did not stop there. We continued our tradition of fair trials. The laws that pertain to this matter before us, such as the law on the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina with relevant amendments, the law on the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the law on the transfer of cases from the ICTY and the use of evidence, the law on the protection of witnesses and vulnerable witnesses, witnesses under threat, and other laws that are related to those primary laws make it possible for us to conduct such proceedings in a very appropriate way. Our law on criminal procedure has been amended, if you compare it to the laws in our neighbouring countries, because we removed the investigative judge from the proceedings and assigned his role to the prosecutor. We also introduced the instrument of plea agreement and this is in use, of course, because it makes proceedings much more speedier, efficient, and less expensive. We are not a high-risk area, as Bosnia and Herzegovina is attempted to be portrayed. There are no terrorist attacks. There are no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other incidents that would distinguish this country from its environment, which is the Balkans. Quite the contrary. We at the state level have tackled all these problems that we face and we have not hesitated to prosecute our high-ranking officials and to convict them, if necessary, including a member of the Presidency or a Supreme Court judge, if indeed he or she is corrupted -- is a corrupt person, or an Interpol representative. The fact that we have corruption trials now for criminal offences committed after the war does not mean that these acts are still committed at the same scale as they were committed after the war. Quite the contrary. By prosecuting such cases, we show that we are ready to tackle problems in our own ranks, all the deviant forms of behaviour that are the legacy of the war in our society. Our laws make it possible for trials to be held without undue delay. We have presented our arguments in our briefs. I would not like to dwell upon that, on the readiness of the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, primarily the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was established in year 2000, and in the 2003 we have -- we had the state prosecutor's office. This is a huge advantage, the fact that we have this court, because this has given us jurisdiction over crimes committed in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We can prosecute them. But let me note that before that we had only partial jurisdiction which was limited to the entities; Republika Srpska, Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Brcko district. Furthermore, I would like to stress that what the learned colleagues from the defence noted, that Article 12 of the law on the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina gives the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has jurisdiction over the most serious crimes the option to allow other lawyers to represent clients before that court, including the lawyers who are not in the registry of the relevant bar associations. I would like to tell you that the rules of procedure are in existence and they regulate this issue, and now it is just a matter of time for the plenary session of the Judges to adopt it formally. And the rule, according to the rules of procedure, international lawyers can represent clients before the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this will be allowed. There will be no exceptions to this rule. As for the objections that witnesses, particularly Defence witnesses, might be in danger that if they come to Bosnia and Herzegovina they face the risk of an arrest, a court issues an arrest warrant, no one else, no other body. But as Bosnia and Herzegovina has already signed a memoranda with its neighbouring countries, with Croatia, for instance, and a similar memoranda will be signed, an agreement will be signed with Serbia and Montenegro on interstate judicial assistance, and as these agreements specify, that witnesses coming to the request country cannot be arrested if they go there as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I -- I apologise for interrupting you. Wouldn't it have been -- I've heard about this memoranda. Wouldn't it have been the simple way just to ratify the European convention on mutual assistance in criminal matters, which is ratified by your neighbour countries as well and would provide a full set, apart from obligations to cooperate which would perhaps ensure that witnesses would be present, but also would provide for the safe conduct you're now referring to, and which is, as far as I understand, in place only with one of your neighbouring countries, and then only in the form of a memorandum. I do not exactly know what status this memorandum would have under international -- public international law. But my question is: Why have so many countries ratified and why have you just signed European convention and not ratified it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the agreements that have been signed or are in the process of being signed, they were signed by prosecutors, state prosecutors in the three countries. They guarantee and they indeed speed up the procedure when it comes to certain requests, especially in terms of interviewing witnesses. And they incorporate provisions of international conventions dealing with this matter. But the prosecutors have greater leeway to act more expeditiously when it comes to gathering evidence. In fact, if you allow, my colleague from the Prosecution can address this because we've also divided our topics amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- yes. I will give her an opportunity to do that. Perhaps then if you could think already about what would have happen if witnesses are living somewhere else where of course a -- where a treaty like European convention would cover a larger area where bilateral treaties, of course, have a limited effect. And secondly, that of course it's always possible to conclude any additional complementary agreement with one of your neighbours, that's well-known and often practiced, but to say this replaces a convention is of course a different matter. So I would just give these questions already for consideration. Please proceed, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Within the context of the reforms carried out in the judiciary of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a registry was set up and very few countries in our immediate neighbourhood and indeed in Europe can boast having that office. The advantages of having a registry in the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina have been great already. As you know, the registry has several departments providing support to the court, the prosecutor's office, the Defence. It provides protection to the witnesses as a department dealing with the PR and so on. And I would like to stress in this context that the international community has invested a lot of resources through various donors' conferences to establish a special chamber at the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina which would be prosecuting war crimes and also the department for organised crime, economic crime, and corruption. The presence of international judges and prosecutors is a guarantee that there will be a high degree of objectivity and impartiality according to our law. The war crimes chambers shall be presided by a domestic judge, but members of the chamber will be international judges. And the proceedings will be conducted in one of the languages of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in English. So apart from these procedural conditions, we also have the material and technical conditions that make it possible for us to conduct such proceedings. From the funds provided by the donors, the court has obtained the most state-of-the-art technology, which makes it possible for the chambers to work efficiently and expeditiously. It is the kind of technology that this court has here. In addition to the legal reasons that our state can put forth when it seeks the referral of these cases to its courts, among those reasons is the fact that the accused are persons that have dual citizenship; their original citizenship being that of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the former Yugoslavia broke down, the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina - Serbs, Bosniaks, and Croats - availed themselves of the possibility to have dual citizenship. Not only Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina or Serbs took the citizenship of Croatia and Serbia respectively, Bosniaks also availed themselves of that right, so many of them have the citizenship both of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina or of Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. So legal grounds that we quote in favour of our argument that we can try our own citizens lies in the fact that their citizenship they obtained by the fact of their birth in Bosnia and Herzegovina is that of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that any other citizenship they may have they obtained after the breakup of the former Yugoslavia. The next grounds that prompt us to seek that these trials be held in Bosnia and Herzegovina lie -- lies in the fact that our Criminal Code stipulates that the criminal legislation of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall apply to everyone who commits a criminal offence in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So we have territorial jurisdiction. The state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina has territorial jurisdiction because the crimes discussed here were committed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina by its citizens, the victims live in the territory of that state, most of the witnesses live in the territory of that state. And finally, justice must be done where the crimes were committed, because victims did not choose where the crime would be committed. Transferring cases such as this one would be particularly detrimental because the process of building trust and creating an atmosphere for the reconciliation of our peoples would be much more difficult. I sometimes say that ten years in prison imposed by a Bosnia and Herzegovina court and 15 years imposed by a court in one of the neighbouring counties, it's not the same because witnesses and victims demand that justice be done there, on the ground where the crimes were committed. If we were to ask ourselves how it would be prejudicial to the accused if this case were to be transferred to the Bosnia and Herzegovina courts, hypothetically speaking this is a perception that people have. But this is the perception, that they would receive a milder sentence if they were to be tried before courts in another state, in this case it would be Serbia and Montenegro. This perception is quite wrong, just as the perception of some of the victims that if a trial is held before a court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they would receive a much stiffer sentence; that would also be wrong. I can tell you that with full responsibility. The standards applied by this court, the standards that have been incorporated in our legislation guarantee a fair trial, as stipulated by the law, without undue delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you -- I said before that we would have approximately half an hour. First of all, I'd like to avoid that this hearing becomes a competition or a race for who wins this case. The Chamber is primarily interested to hear about all kind of legal technical matters, and of course we are aware, just as has been shown by both the Prosecution and the Defence, and I hear it in your words as well, of course these legal, technical matters are not on its own. They all serve the final purpose of fair trials for those who are accused, for a fair justice for those who are victims, so therefore these technicalities are not to be viewed as isolated elements, but at the same time they are very important because they all serve the same purpose. What I heard until now that you mainly took the general approach of it. To the extent possible I would like to give -- and we have not much more than ten minutes left, but we will continue tomorrow in the afternoon briefly. If there is any specific matter that you would like to address at this moment, please do so. And I take it that on the technical matters we'll get more information, perhaps briefly tomorrow, by those assigned to give us that information. Is there any specific matter you would like to draw our attention to at this very moment, any further matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to draw your attention to a point that my colleague will discuss in greater detail, and that is that the Criminal Code of the SFRY of 1977 prescribed in Articles 30 that a criminal act can be committed by an act or a failure to act. It further provides that a criminal act can be committed by a failure to act only when the perpetrator has failed to carry out an act that he was duty-bound to perform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. This is mainly in the field of command responsibility. We'd like to hear, but we can't do that in a couple of minutes, to hear some further details in that respect. And we especially are interested to know to what extent also negligence would be covered by these legal provisions, because that might be a problem. I would suggest that we leave some of the technical aspects but then very concise for tomorrow in the afternoon, if that would be suitable for you. Is there another matter which you would like to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to take advantage of this time now because my colleagues would like to say something. Ms. Mechtild Lauth would like to say something about command responsibility, by your leave, or shall we leave that until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest that we leave this technical matters for tomorrow, and I take it that then because you have been in the procedure at least you know what part of our problems are, if you can deal with that in 10 to 12 minutes, if that would be possible. If you write it down, apart from presenting it in an oral way, that would be good as well. Yes? Madam President, anything else? Because we will then take time tomorrow to listen to it and it's earlier on the day, which keeps us fresher as well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, that we leave it until tomorrow, in view of the brevity of time left to us for our presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Perhaps while we are waiting, can I raise this: For the sake of the record, Madam President, the transcript says that you said, in page 76 from line 16 to 17, I quote: "Transferring cases such as this one would be particularly detrimental because" -- blah, blah, blah. But that is quite opposite to what you are saying. Could you remember what you did say at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be detrimental to the confidence-building process or the process of the restoration of confidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is detrimental, transferring the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRESO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is to say, the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, are quite able. And I have to point out that the war devastated our judicial system, and if such cases are referred to us, we are given a chance - and I appeal to you, Your Honours, to do this - give us a chance to prove not only to the people at home but also the international community that we are able to look the truth in the face and that we are able to issue both convictions and acquittals, that we are able to justify the confidence that the international community has placed in us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Kreso. I think I can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would like to thank you very much, Madam President, for addressing us, and we'll hear on technical details further tomorrow. I'd like, then, as the last part of this hearing to address you, Mr. Loncar, representative of Serbia and Montenegro. I would say the same would apply for you, that I leave it up to you whether you will start with any technical comments or with a rather general comment. You may have noticed that, as I said before, that this Chamber would be -- would try to avoid this to become a race for the case and try to avoid that this would be competition of who would best do the case. The Chamber is convinced that there is a -- there is much at stake, both for Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also we know that some of the occasions ask for a referral to Serbia and Montenegro, so therefore you'll be here as a party soon in other cases perhaps as well. But we'd like to -- not to make it a competition for who gets away here with the case. So if you would please address the Court and perhaps give additional information or additional thoughts on the submissions you've already made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, seeing that we are coming near to the end of today's session and that there are only about ten minutes left, I wish to address you on general issues and tomorrow we can discuss specific issues. Therefore, allow me at the outset, Your Honours, to express the gratitude of my government for inviting us to attend today's session and making it possible for us to address you on this important matter. Also, at the outset I wish to express the political will of my government to fully cooperate with the International Criminal Tribunal and the readiness of my government to have some of the cases pending before this Tribunal tried before our national judiciary. Serbia and Montenegro is properly prepared and I believe able to try all those suspected of war crimes. I think that this is best supported by the opinion of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. In the 11 bis motion for transferral submitted in the case of Vladimir Kovacevic of the 28th of October, 2004, in paragraphs 41 to 45 stated the following: "Serbia and Montenegro possess the political will and is properly prepared to prosecute the accused before its own courts. The prosecutor has developed excellent working relations with the Belgrade district court in relation to war crimes cases. In cooperation with the ICTY Prosecutor, the war crimes prosecutor of the Republic of Serbia brought indictments against a number of persons suspected of participating in the massacre at Ovcara and actively cooperated with the office of the ICTY Prosecutor in bringing other cases to trial. As a result, the ICTY Prosecutor transferred to the Belgrade district court one case of a war crime committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Prosecutor believed the Belgrade district court, its judges, and the war crimes prosecutor had the skills and technical capabilities to prosecute the Vladimir Kovacevic case according to the internationally recognised standards of justice. The ICTY prosecutor was further satisfied that the accused would receive a fair trial." Allow me, in support of my government's claim, to put forward the submission that the crimes alleged against the accused were not committed in Serbia and therefore there are no passions around that might influence the prosecutor and the judges. As for political will, the political will of Serbia and Montenegro to try war crimes cases, let me say again that the governments are fully committed to cooperation with the ICTY. This cooperation has intensified after the enactment of the law enacted two years ago in 2003 by which a special Chamber for war crimes was established with the district Belgrade court as well as a special war crimes prosecutor. Both bodies have in a short time shown excellent results in war crimes prosecutions and this has been recognised by all independent observers. Serbia and Montenegro and Serbia are institutionally and legislatively ready, willing to prosecute cases of serious violations of international humanitarian law on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Let me reiterate that for the reconciliation of the peoples of the former Yugoslavia, it would be of exceptional importance for every country to try its own citizens, because this would demonstrate its maturity, its willingness to face its own past and the crimes allegedly committed on its behalf. This is the only way for the judgements to be widely accepted by the domestic public. If the accused and their Defence counsel do not have confidence in the judiciary of one country, then their compatriots may reject the truth established by that court. And the ICTY for a time in the public opinion of the former Yugoslavia was mistrusted, without going into the merits of the cases and the judgements handed down in that period. It seems to be in the interest of Serbia and also in the interest of Bosnia and Herzegovina that this case be prosecuted in Belgrade. This would be the best way to grapple with the past, a past that is burdening all the states on the territory of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the former Yugoslavia. Your Honours, allow me to put forward the standpoint of my government, which is that we fully support the arguments regarding extradition put forward by Defence counsel Lukic today. As for specific technical details, I hope that we will have further opportunity tomorrow to hear my colleagues speak on these matters. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Loncar. First of all, I have to apologise to the interpreters. I didn't ask the permission to go on longer than we intended to do. So apologies for that. Now, Mr. Loncar, perhaps since you expressed as your view that since the crimes had not been committed in Serbia and Montenegro that there would be less passion in such a trial, but this of course -- perhaps your colleague could give it some thought overnight -- is this a frontal attack against the principle of territoriality which usually you say is that the primary jurisdiction that should deal with the matter, that's the jurisdiction of the place where it happened. Some might say that if you go far away from where it all happened that perhaps the voice of the victims might not be heard anymore and that there could be compassion for other reasons, perhaps not primarily the compassion with the victims which might result in a judgement which -- well, might be too heavy. But of course there's the shadow side of the same problem, that if there is any -- if there is compassion with the accused, then it of course could also result in a judgement which would be considered too lenient, at least by the victims. So therefore, it's -- to say it didn't happen here so there's no passion, that seems to be a -- well, I consider it a bit simplistic as an approach for a rather complex problem. We'll adjourn until tomorrow as quarter past 2.00. Both governments will have time to address the technical matters. Finally, the parties -- and if you could do it together, that would be fine -- will have an opportunity to make some final comments to the extent necessary. And you may have noticed especially also what kind of subjects the Chamber is specifically interested in. I might say a few words as well, and we hope to finish tomorrow in a little bit over one hour, so altogether perhaps three-quarters of an hour. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same court.
